This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 119 columns across 9 data files.
#### Issues Identified

3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

text.text: Food learning in early life largely relies on social learning.
Previous research has shown that infants learn something is edible when they directly observe someone else eating it.
However, the role of other forms of food-related social information remains largely unknown.
Food processing actions (e.g., chopping, mashing) are essential components of human food behaviors and a ubiquitous part of infants' everyday lives.

Here we examined whether infants (i) differentially attend to eating and food processing actions compared to control actions and (ii) learn that novel foods are edible after observing eating and food processing actions performed with them.
We tested 12-month-olds' responses to three different actions: eating, food processing, and a control action (touch).

First, we showed infants side-by-side videos of an adult performing two different actions with novel foods across three between-subjects conditions and measured their gaze and pupil dilation with an eye-tracker.
Then, we offered infants the novel foods shown in the videos and measured their choices and eating behaviors.

Our eye-tracking results indicate that infants differentially attend to eating and food processing actions relative to the control action, and show increased pupil dilation for the control action relative to the two actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting).
When asked to choose which novel food they could eat, infants chose the novel food they saw an actor eat, but only when that eating action was paired with the control action.
These findings help identify important mechanisms that increase acceptance of healthy foods early in life.
Eating a balanced diet rich in healthy foods like fruits and vegetables is essential for good health (Wirt & Collins, 2009).

text.text: Developing healthy eating habits is especially important in the first years of life because many food habits and preferences are acquired early in development and are associated with dietary patterns in later childhood and adulthood (Luque et al., 2018; Nicklaus et al., 2005).

Food neophobia-the avoidance of novel foods-is well known to occur during early childhood.

text.text: Therefore, it is important to understand how children learn about novel foods in order to identify specific mechanisms that increase acceptance of healthy foods early in life.

While individual learning plays an important role in the development of food preferences in infancy and childhood (e.g., via flavor-flavor learning [FFL] or flavor-nutrient learning [FNL], in which a new food is paired with a flavor or nutrient that is already liked; see Mura-Paroche et al., 2017 for a review), we focus here on social learning processes.

text.text: Therefore, it seems that food learning in infancy and early childhood is based on a set of specific actions that can indicate edibility and, as a consequence, not all social information about food has the potential to decrease infants' and children's food avoidance behaviors.
The effects of watching someone else eat a food on infants' and young children's food learning and avoidance behaviors has been well studied (see e.g., DeJesus et al., 2018, Rioux, 2019 for reviews).

text.text: However, the effects of other forms of food-related social information remain largely uninvestigated.
One form of social information that deserves further investigation is food processing.
Here we define food processing as actions that alter the naturally occurring state of foods (e.g., an apple growing on its tree), such as cutting, grinding, or cooking.

These processing techniques have been an important part of human life for millennia (Wrangham, 2009) and are still the main techniques applied to the foods in human societies (e.g., Mombo et al., 2016).

text.text: Food processing is a prior and often necessary step for human food consumption.
For example, foods like breads, stews, cakes, etc. do not exist until naturally occurring foods are processed, sometimes in elaborate ways.
Therefore, cues of processing are reliable social signals about what kinds of entities are consumed within the local environment.

Consistent with this view, adults and children from three years of age view processed foods (e.g., foods cooked and pureed) as human-made objects that bear markers of previous human intervention, while they view unprocessed foods as naturally occurring (Foroni et al., 2013; Girgis & Nguyen, 2020).

text.text: In addition, adults view processed foods as being more ready to eat than unprocessed foods (Foroni et al., 2013).

text.text: Similarly, children miscategorized non-food items (e.g., pieces of wood) that have been sliced into pieces as foods (Foinant et al., 2021a), suggesting that children are more likely to think something that has been cut is a food.

text.text: These results indicate that adults and young children use cues of food processing to infer that another person has already interacted with a candidate food and has deemed it to be edible.
However, it is not yet known whether infants make this same inference.
Another important aspect of food processing is that many processing techniques reduce the toxicity of raw food items.
For example, cassava root is a staple food in many societies, but it cannot be eaten raw and requires complex processing techniques to be consumed without a risk of poisoning (Mombo et al., 2016).

text.text: It is therefore possible that, in addition to serving as a potential social signal of edibility, cues of food processing also indicate that processed food items are safe to handle, which would decrease avoidance behaviors.
Accordingly, children assign negative properties (e.g., "This food makes you throw up") less often to processed foods compared to unprocessed foods (Foinant et al., 2021b).

text.text: Importantly, in previous studies of food processing, infants and young children did not witness the acts of food processing directly (Foinant et al., 2021a (Foinant et al., , 2021b;; Foroni et al., 2013; Girgis & Nguyen, 2020; Rioux & Wertz, 2021).

text.text: Instead, they were presented with foods that had already been processed (e.g., foods cooked and pureed, or cut into pieces) and were able to infer the previous human intervention.
Therefore, infants' responses to the food processing actions themselves remain unknown.
The existing literature indicates that watching what others eat and seeing evidence of food processing are important aspects of human food learning.
However, two broad questions remain unanswered.
The first question is whether infants are particularly attentive to eating and food processing actions when learning about food.
It is well established that infants differentially attend to certain types of important stimuli or actions (e.g., Golinkoff et al., 2013).

text.text: But what about eating and food processing actions?
There are a number of reasons why infants may pay particular attention to someone performing eating and food processing actions.

Infants learn that a particular entity is edible after observing an adult putting it in the mouth, but not when the adult handled it in other ways (e.g., placing it behind the ear, holding it in front of the face and expressing negative affect; Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019) and it is possible that they will also differentially attend to this eating action.

text.text: Similarly, infants' attention may be drawn by food processing actions because they may also serve as indicators of edibility, or a signal that a food can be handled (e.g., Foinant et al., 2021b; Rioux & Wertz, 2021).

text.text: Therefore, the current experiment tested whether infants differentially attend to eating and food processing actions relative to a control action.
The second question is whether infants perceive social cues of food processing as cues about the edibility of the foods per se.
Previous results indicate that infants are more willing to approach and handle processed foods.

For example, Rioux & Wertz (2021) presented 7-to 15month-old infants with unprocessed whole plants and processed plant foods (e.g., unfamiliar fruits and vegetables cut into pieces) and found a reduced reluctance to touch and eat processed plant foods compared to whole plants.

text.text: However, the existing work was not designed to assess eating behaviors, that is, whether infants put the different items in their mouth, so it is not yet clear whether infants use food processing actions as a cue of edibility.

The aim of the current experiment is to investigate whether infants (i) differentially attend to eating and food processing actions compared to a control action and (ii) choose and attempt to eat (i.e., put in their mouth) novel foods after observing eating and food processing actions performed with them.
To answer these questions, we conducted an experiment with 12-month-old infants using a combination of a preferential looking time paradigm and a choice paradigm.
Infants were first presented with a split-screen presentation of an adult performing different actions on novel foods (the Action Presentation Phase).
During the Action Presentation Phase, infants were divided into three between-subjects conditions.
In each condition, infants saw a different pairing of two actions.
These pairings were created from combinations of three possible actions: eating, a food processing action (cutting), and a control action (touching).
Two of these actions-eating and cutting-may indicate edibility, while the touching action served as a control for lowerlevel features of the other actions.
The eating action was an adult lifting a novel food with a pair of tongs to her mouth and consuming a bite of it.
The cutting action was an adult chopping a novel food into pieces with a knife.

We used cutting as our food processing action because (i) cutting is a typical food processing action that is also a common component of many more complex food processing techniques and (ii) previous work has shown that infants and young children can distinguish between cut and whole foods (Foinant et al., 2021b; Rioux & Wertz, 2021), which makes cutting a suitable action to use with infants.

text.text: The touch control action was an adult holding a novel food with a shoe horn and touching the food with her finger.

In order to control for the necessary presence of a knife in the cutting action, we ensured that each action included an artifact: tongs in the eating action, a knife in the cutting action, and a shoe horn in the touch control action.

Combining these actions into pairs led to three between-subjects conditions, each showing an alternating set of action videos: 1) eating vs. touching, 2) cutting vs. touching, and 3) eating vs. cutting.

Infants' gaze was recorded with an eye-tracker to determine (i) which actions they look at longer and (ii) their pupillary changes in response to each display, as infants' interest in a stimulus can be indexed by increased pupil dilation (Ackermann et al., 2019; Hepach & Westermann, 2016).

text.text: After the Action Presentation Phase of the experiment, infants in all conditions were presented with the two novel foods shown in the videos and asked "Which one can you eat?"
(Choice Phase).
We recorded which novel food the infants subsequently chose (i.e., the first novel food they touched using a visually-guided reach) and attempted to eat (i.e., put in their mouth).
All infants were presented with the same choice procedure, regardless of the action types presented in their between-subjects condition.

Infants saw intact versions of the novel foods during the Choice Phase that did not show any traces of the actions performed in the Action Presentation Phase (e.g., pieces missing from cutting or eating).

We did this because our interest in the present study was the identity of a novel food (i.e., that it was associated with a particular action type), not changes in its quantity or appearance (see e.g., Cheries et al., 2008).

text.text: The existing literature suggests several possible interpretations of pupil dilation measures.

Specifically, phasic pupil dilation, which occurs in immediate response to a stimulus, has been established as a measure of arousal and cognitive load (e.g., Hepach & Westermann, 2016; Steinhauer et al., 2022).

text.text: We describe our pupil dilation findings in terms of cognitive load, but we acknowledge that at least one (if not more) of these underlying processes are likely to be involved.
We had two main predictions.

First, if infants differentially attend to actions that could indicate edibility (eating and cutting), we predicted that infants would exhibit longer looking times and increased pupil dilation in response to the eating and cutting actions compared to the control action in the Action Presentation Phase (Prediction 1).

Second, if infants learn that novel foods are edible by seeing eating and food processing actions performed on them, we predicted that infants would choose and eat the novel food item shown in the eating and cutting action videos in the Choice Phase (Prediction 2).
Based on the existing research outlined above, we expected that infants would view our eating action as a cue of edibility.

Our experimental design allowed us to assess whether infants treat a food processing "cutting" action similarly to the eating action or, alternatively, if they treat it similarly to the touch control action.

Participants' gaze was measured with an EyeLink1000 eye-tracker (SR Research Ltd) in remote mode, which is suitable for unrestrained infants.

The camera was positioned in front of the infant at a distance of approximately 60 cm (EyeLink 1000 User Manual, 2010).

After positioning the infant and caregiver in front of the eye-tracker, an experimenter stepped behind a curtain from where the infant and caregiver could be monitored on a video screen and started the experiment.
The testing session consisted of two parts: an Action Presentation Phase using a preferential looking time paradigm and a Choice Phase using a manual forced-choice paradigm.

Preferential looking time paradigms have been used successfully with infants for decades, including eye-tracking methods, as have manual forced-choice paradigms (e.g., Aslin, 2007; DeJesus et al., 2015; Hamlin et al., 2007; Hamlin & Wynn, 2011; Golinkoff et al., 2013; Stahl & Feigenson, 2015; Wertz & Wynn, 2014; Wertz & Wynn, 2019).

After an eye-tracking calibration sequence (not pictured), infants first saw the Action Presentation Phase (top panel) during which we assessed infants' visual attention and pupil dilation.
This phase began with a still image of the two novel food stimuli (black carrots and white parsnip; Panel 1 "Root Still 1").
Next, infants saw a sequence of alternating videos of two different actions shown on opposite sides of the screen (Panel 2 "Video of Action 1" and Panel 3 "Video of Action 2").
Each of the two action videos was repeated three times resulting in a total of six trials; there were three between-subjects conditions of different action pairings: Eat vs.
Touch, Eat vs.
Cut, Cut vs.
Touch (condition Eat vs.
Cut is depicted here).
Next, infants were shown a side-by-side image of stills from each action video (Panel 4 "Action Still") followed by another still image of the novel foods (Panel 5 "Root Still 2").

The final phase of the experiment was the Choice Phase (bottom panel) in which an experimenter who was blind to the condition acted as if they were "picking" the novel foods from the screen (Panel 6) and then offered the two real novel foods to the infants (Panel 7); We assessed infants' choices (i.e., the first root they touched with a visually-guided reach) and eating behavior (i.e., which root they put in their mouth).
The study ended with a Choice Phase (see Fig. 1, bottom panel).

text.text: At the beginning of this phase, an experimenter, who was blind to the action performed with each root type, emerged from behind a curtain and then reached toward the screen that still showed the two piles of roots from Root Still 2.

The experimenter gave the illusion of picking up one root from each of the piles, presenting two real roots to the infant (see Fig. 1, Panel 6; adapted from Kinzler et al., 2007; DeJesus et al., 2015).

text.text: Importantly, during the Choice Phase, all infants were presented with whole roots that did not show traces of the actions performed on them during the Action Presentation Phase.
We selected intact, whole roots for two reasons.
First, this ensured that the roots were identical in size and did not provide visual cues about the previously observed actions (e.g., missing pieces resulting from eating or cutting).
Second, it encouraged infants to track object identity rather than appearance.

This distinction between identity and appearance is important because changes in appearance can affect infants' and young children's representations of objects (Cheries et al., 2008 , Keil, 1989 , Piaget et al., 1960).
text.formatted: This distinction between identity and appearance is important because changes in appearance can affect infants' and young children's representations of objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cheries et al., 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">, Keil, 1989</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">, Piaget et al., 1960)</ref>.

text.text: For example, in the classic conservation-of-mass task, young children often report that changing an object's shape (e.g., flattening a ball of clay) changes its mass (i.e., the child will say the flatted ball has more clay than the round ball; Piaget et al., 1960).

text.text: Using intact roots allowed us to investigate the identity of a root (i.e., that it was associated with a particular action) independent of changes to its quantity or appearance.

This approach is consistent with evidence showing that, although infants fail to track object quantity when a food (a cracker) is split into two pieces, they maintain a representation of its identity (Cheries et al., 2008).

At the end of their verbal prompt, the experimenter moved the two roots forward within the infants' reach.
If infants were reluctant to choose, the experimenter repeated the questions.
Infants' choices were coded as the first root they touched while looking at it (i.e., their first visually-guided reach, as in Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019).

text.text: Infants' eating behaviors were coded as whether or not they brought the root in contact with their mouth.
For safety reasons, we did not let infants bite the root and recorded only infants' attempts to put the root in their mouth.
If infants did not touch either of the roots after 60 s, the session ended.
Caregivers were asked to keep their eyes closed throughout the Choice Phase to prevent them from influencing infants' behavior.

Infants were randomly assigned to one of three between-subjects conditions that differed in the pairings of actions presented during the Action Presentation Phase; the Choice Phase was the same across conditions.
(1) Condition1 = Eat vs.
Touch Actions (N = 27).
This condition investigated whether infants preferentially attend to eating actions compared to a control action.
Infants were shown an actor eating one root stimulus in one video (see Fig. 2, Panel A) and touching the other root stimulus in the other video (see Fig. 2, Panel B).
text.formatted: Infants were shown an actor eating one root stimulus in one video (see Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>, Panel A) and touching the other root stimulus in the other video (see Fig. <ref type="figure">2</ref>, Panel B).

text.text: In the eating action video, an actor was seated at a table behind one root type.
The actor first greeted the infant, then lifted the root in front of her using a pair of tongs, grabbed the root with her other hand and placed it in her mouth.
The tongs were included to control for the presence of a knife in the cutting action video (described below).
The actor took two bites, returned the root to the table with her hand, and placed her hand next to it.
In the touch action video, the same actor was seated behind the other root type.
The actor greeted infants, then held the root using a shoehorn (to control for the presence of a tool) and touched the food with her finger.

She then moved her hand up and tucked her hair behind her ear to match the low-level features of the eating action (i.e., a hand moving up towards the face, performing a natural-looking action, and moving down again).
We used an eating action because infants use this action to learn about edibility (e.g., Liberman et al., 2016; Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019).
text.formatted: We used an eating action because infants use this action to learn about edibility (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Liberman et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wertz & Wynn, 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We used the touch action as a control action that, taken on its own, does not indicate the edibility of an object because infants routinely see their caregivers touching a wide variety of objects, including food and non-food, but is also a familiar action for infants.

The advantage of using a familiar action as a control compared to an unfamiliar action closely matched for low-level features (e.g., putting the food behind the ear; Wertz & Wynn, 2014) is that it removes potential confounds from the preferential looking method (i.e., infants looking longer to unfamiliar actions; see e.g., Aslin, 2007) and from the pupil dilation measure (i.e., infants showing increased pupil dilation to surprising events; Hepach & Westermann, 2016).

Touch Actions (N = 28).
This condition tested whether infants preferentially attend to food processing actions and view them as a cue of edibility.
Infants were shown a video of an actor slicing one root type in front of her with a knife (see Fig. 2, Panel C) paired with a video of the actor touching the other root type.

text.text: In the video displaying a cutting action, after greeting the infant, the actor held the root with one hand while cutting slices two times with the knife using her other hand.
At the end of the video, the actor tucked her hair behind her ear (to match the low-level features of the eating action).

The touch action was the same one described above and, as in Condition 1, the touch action here serves as a low-level familiar control action that allows us to determine whether infants respond differently to foodprocessing actions (cutting) compared to any kind of contact (touching).

text.text: In order to assess whether infants' prior food experiences or eating behaviors may affect their responses, we asked parents to complete a battery of five questionnaires.
All questionnaires were completed online, either before or after the lab session.
The first questionnaire assessed infant's familiarity with the different stimuli presented in the study (i.e., black carrot, parsnip and white parsley root, knife, tongs, shoehorn)foot_0 .
text.formatted: The first questionnaire assessed infant's familiarity with the different stimuli presented in the study (i.e., black carrot, parsnip and white parsley root, knife, tongs, shoehorn)<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> .

text.text: In the experiment infants saw black carrot and parsnip but we also asked about white parsley root as it is very similar-looking to parsnip.

Parents were asked: (i) whether their infant has ever seen these six objects (Yes/No) (ii) how often their infant interacts with these objects (from never to nearly every day) and (iii) how often their infant sees their parent interacting with these objects (from never to nearly every day).

The stimuli were chosen to be a priori unfamiliar to infants and results from this questionnaire confirmed our assumption: Familiarity with black carrots M = 2.74, familiarity with parsley roots M = 3.58, familiarity with parsnip M = 5.85; Ratings could range from 0 (Infants never saw, interacted or saw their caregivers interacting with the object) to 15 (Infants saw, interact and see their caregivers interacting with the object every day).
The second questionnaire asked about food consumption at home and age of introduction to fruits and vegetables.

Parents were asked how often their infant eats 10 typical German foods at home (i.e., milk, dairy products, bread, cereals, fresh fruits and vegetables, meat, fish, sweet products, savory snacks, ready-to-eat foods).
Their responses were rated on a nine-point Likert scale (0 = never to9 = more than five times a day).
Parents were also asked at what age they introduce in their infant's diet the following foods: Infant formula, pureed foods, fresh fruits and vegetables, cereal products, meat and family foods.
The third questionnaire was the Children's Feeding and Eating Difficulties Questionnaire (Rigal et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The third questionnaire was the Children's Feeding and Eating Difficulties Questionnaire <ref type="bibr">(Rigal et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This questionnaire is divided into three parts.
The first part contains twelve questions and asks parents about their infant's attitude about food (e.g., "My child looks forward to mealtimes").
Their responses were rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Very wrong to5 = Very true).
The second part contains seventeen questions and asks parents about their feeding practices (e.g., "During mealtimes, when your child hesitates to taste a food, does it happen that you get angry?").
Their responses were rated on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = Never to5 = Always).

The last part contains twenty-one questions and asks parents about what they do when they are confronted with different feeding situations (e.g., "Your child wants to eat pasta when you intended to cook vegetables.
You stick to your idea of vegetables without trying to negotiate.").
Their responses were rated on a 4-point Likert scale (1 = Very unlikely to4 = Very likely).
The fourth questionnaire was the Child Food Rejection Scale (Rioux et al., 2017), which directly assesses children's food neophobic and picky eating behaviors.
text.formatted: The fourth questionnaire was the Child Food Rejection Scale <ref type="bibr">(Rioux et al., 2017)</ref>, which directly assesses children's food neophobic and picky eating behaviors.

text.text: Six questions are related to food neophobia (e.g., "My child always chooses familiar food").
Five questions are related to pickiness (e.g., "My child refuses to eat some foods because of their texture").
Parents' responses were rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree to5 = Strongly agree).
The last questionnaire assessed socio-demographic characteristics of the two parents.
Specifically, parents were asked about their level of education, as a proxy for social-economic status.
This approach is commonly used in studies examining correlates of food rejection (Cole et al., 2017).

text.text: First, parents were asked if each parent has a general school-education qualification.
If this was the case, they were asked about the level of school education they had received.
Next, they were asked about professional education, and last about their highest qualification, with options ranging from vocational internship to PhD.
Answers were then transformed into the ordered variable Years of Education, ranging from 10 years (intermediate level of maturity or "Mittlere Reife") to 21 years (PhD).

text.text: In order to test whether infants differentially attended to actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting) than by the control action, we examined infants' looking behavior and pupil dilation during the Action Presentation Phase (see showed the goal of each action (e.g., root in the mouth, knife cutting the root, finger touching the root; still images are shown in Fig 2).

The analysis of the Action Still looking times assessed whether infants' attention remained differentially captured by the eating and cutting actions after the dynamic action video sequences had concluded.
For the Root Stills, infants saw the same still image of the roots twice during the presentation.

The first time infants saw the Root Still was before any action was performed on the two roots (see Fig.1 Panel 1) and the second time they saw the Root Still was after infants saw the videos of different actions performed on the two types of roots (see Fig 1 Panel 5).

We measured the change in infants' looking time for both roots across the two time points (i.e., the mean looking time during the second Root Still minus mean looking time during the first Root Still).
The analysis of the Root Still looking times tested whether infants' visual attention to a novel root stimulus was influenced by having previously observed eating and cutting actions performed on it.
For both the Action Still and Root Stills, we tested the significance of the following predictors: Action (Eat, Cut, Touch), Condition ("Eat vs.
Touch", "Cut vs.
Touch", "Eat vs.
Cut"), Sex (Male, Female) and Age (continuous factor).
In the final models, infant participants served as a random factor.
Action, Condition, Sex and Age were modeled as fixed effects.
The model for Action stills will hereafter be referred to as Model 2, while the model for Root still will hereafter be referred to as Model 3.
Third, we ran another linear mixed-effect model with infants' pupil dilation as the dependent variable.
Pupil dilation was assessed during the period from 400 ms to 2000 ms after each Action Video, when gaze rested on identical attention grabbers (see Fig 1., Panels 2 and 3).

text.text: Pupil dilation data were obtained using the following preprocessing steps: (i) Sampling rate reduction: Our eye-tracking data was assessed at a 500 Hz sampling rate (see Section 2.3.
Apparatus above).

Because in infant studies eye-trackers with a sampling rate of 60 Hz are more common (e.g., Tobii eye-tracking systems), we reduced our data to 60Hz in the pupil-dilation analysis to make it comparable to the results of other pupil dilation studies.

(ii) Baseline correction and standardization: Because participants naturally differ in their individual baseline pupil sizes, pupil data was baseline-corrected within each infant by subtracting the median of the individual's data from each of its values, respectively.
Additionally, pupil data was standardized (following procedures suggested by Mathôt et al., 2018) to obtain our dependent variable of pupil dilation.

text.text: Note that the raw units of pupil size on which this procedure is based are arbitrary units, as is common in EyeLink systems (EyeLink 1000 User Manual, 2010).
Following the same approach as with our looking time data, we tested the significance of the following predictors: Action (Eat, Cut, Touch), Condition ("Eat vs.
Touch", "Cut vs.

Cut"), Trial (1 → 6), Sex (Male, Female), Age, Horizontal and Vertical gaze position and Head distance to the screen (continuous factors).
Direction of gaze and eye distance can affect pupil size measurement and are therefore suggested to be included as control variables in pupil dilation analyses (Gagl et al., 2011).

text.text: We included Trial to gain insight into whether infants show an increase or decrease in cognitive load as indexed by changes in pupil dilation, after repeated presentations of each action type.
Note that each individual infant only saw three repetitions of an action video, therefore the trial variable includes both within-and between-subjects data.
Condition also did not contribute to the model and was removed to avoid overfitting.
In the final model, infant participants served as a random factor, as did video side (left vs. right) and Trial under the condition of participant.
Action (Eat, Cut, Touch), Trial (1 → 6), Sex (Male, Female), Age, Horizontal and Vertical gaze position and Head distance to the screen (continuous factors) were modeled as fixed effects.
This model will hereafter be referred to as Model 4.
Finally, we ran linear mixed-effects models with infants' pupil dilation as the dependent variable and adding the interaction term Action*Trial to the model.

Because a significant interaction would indicate that differences between action types vary across trials, this additional exploratory analysis was conducted to better understand the timeline of cognitive load elicited by the repeated presentations of the different action types.
In this model, infant participants served as a random factor, as did video side (left vs. right) and Trial under the condition of participant.

Action (Eat, Cut, Touch), Trial (1 → 6), Action*Trial, Sex (Male, Female), Age, Horizontal and Vertical gaze position and Head distance to the screen (continuous factors) were modeled as fixed effects.

The aim of this study was to investigate whether 12-month-old infants (i) differentially attend to actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting) compared to a control action (touching), and (ii) choose and attempt to eat (i.e., put in their mouth) novel foods after observing eating and food processing actions performed with them.
Our results show that 12-month-old infants did indeed look longer at eating and cutting actions than at the touch control action.
Infants show this pattern of response to the action videos, but not when static images of the same actions were presented.
Moreover, infants exhibited the greatest pupil dilation in response to the touch control action.
After watching the action videos and being asked "Which one can you eat?"
infants chose the novel food they had seen an adult eat, but only when that eating action was paired with the touch control action.

The current results demonstrate that, while infants were interested in all actions, they exhibit longer looking times when attending to actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting) compared to the control action (touching).
This difference was constant across trials (i.e., for looking time data, the Action*Trial interaction did not improve model fit, unlike for the pupil data).
This pattern supports our first prediction and adds to existing research showing that infants differentially attend to important stimuli or actions (e.g., Golinkoff et al., 2013).

text.text: Importantly, our findings add a novel dimension to our understanding of social learning about food in infancy: The set of specific actions infants attend to when interacting with food includes food processing actions like cutting.

In fact, infants pay similar attention to someone cutting a food and someone eating a food, which is an established cue of edibility (e.g., Liberman et al., 2016; Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019), despite the fact that our cutting action shares more lowlevel features with the touch control action.

text.text: Future studies could investigate whether variation in infants' everyday exposure to food processing actions influences their attention to these actions.
While some infants routinely observe their caregivers preparing food, others may have fewer opportunities to do so.
Our results also showed that infants exhibit the greatest overall pupil dilation in response to the touch control action.

This finding may seem at odds with our claim that infants attend to actions that may indicate edibility more than the control action as infants' attention towards a stimulus has been found to be indexed by increased pupil dilation (Ackermann et al., 2019; Hepach & Westermann, 2016).

text.text: An alternative interpretation is that infants attend more to eating and cutting actions in order to learn about potential food items, but were to some degree puzzled by our touch control action.

In fact, previous studies have found that infants can show increased pupil dilation when they observe a surprising event (e.g., someone bringing a spoon to the hand instead of bringing it to the mouth, Gredebäck & Melinder, 2010) and that pupil dilation reflect both infants' interest and surprise (Hepach & Westermann, 2016; Jackson & Sirois, 2022).

text.text: The touch action we used as a control does not indicate edibility per se and infants routinely see their caregivers touching both food and non-food objects.

However, to match the three different actions we tested for low-level features (e.g., length of the action sequences, use of a metal tool in all actions), we used a touch action that involved stroking the novel food with one finger while holding it to the table with a metal shoehorn-which might have been particularly unexpected for infants.
Future studies could use different control actions that are not likely to indicate edibility, and are also not surprising.
Our analysis of the pupil data across the consecutive trials revealed interesting differences that could reconcile our looking time and pupil dilation findings (see Fig. 5).

text.text: Specifically, pupil dilation evolved differently across trials depending on the action type: dilation for both the eating and cutting actions increased over the trials, while dilation for the touch control action did not significantly change across the trials.
Mean pupil size for all actions was close to baseline during the first action video in our presentation, but changed when the second action was presented.

Since the touch control action in the second trial was always preceded by an action that may indicate edibility (eating or cutting), and the eating and cutting actions may share more similarities (e.g., the conceptual content of indicating edibility, or being seen as more familiar or less unusual than the touch control action), seeing a touch action following an eating or cutting action might have violated infants' expectations more than seeing a cutting action following an eating action or vice versa.
Pupil size reflects immediate responses to events, and is therefore seen as a more precise measure of cognitive processes than looking time (Jackson & Sirois, 2009).

text.text: Thus, the differently evolving trajectories of pupil dilation for the action types over trials may indicate that, even if the touch control action was consistently surprising to infants, the combination of actions that may indicate edibility of a novel food were of increasing interest across trials (e.g., Chen & Westermann, 2018).

text.text: Additionally, the increase in pupil dilation for the eating and cutting actions as trials progressed might indicate that infants were actively learning about these actions (e.g., Ackermann et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2019).

text.text: In their study, increased pupil size in 13-month-olds after the presentation of a stimulus predicted greater learning success.

Interestingly, looking time, which was assessed during stimulus presentation, neither predicted learning success nor correlated with pupil dilation (Cheng et al., 2019), suggesting discrepancies between looking time as a measure of more general interest and pupil dilation as an indication of the more differentiated processes of learning or surprise.

text.text: In any case, taken together, our pupil dilation and looking time results show that infants respond differently to the eating and cutting actions than to the touch control action.

The previous literature indicates that eating actions are particularly influential because they serve as cues of edibility (Liberman et al., 2014; Rioux & Wertz, 2026; Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019), and the current results suggest that food processing actions may be viewed similarly.

text.text: Food processing actions might capture infants' attention because these actions transform a novel (food) item into something that more closely resembles food items that are more familiar to them (since infants are typically first introduced to pureed or cut foods).
Learning about food involves distinguishing between what is edible and what is not (Mura-Paroche et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Learning about food involves distinguishing between what is edible and what is not <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Mura-Paroche et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In this sense, food processing actions might help infants identify food items by signaling that the whole, unfamiliar food object they observe being processed is the same as the pureed/cut foods they already know.

Although our eye-tracking data shows that infants react to the eating and cutting actions more similarly than the touch action, our choice data suggest that infants may make different inferences from eating and cutting actions depending on the context in which they occur.

Infants chose the food they saw an actor eat when this occurred in the context of the touch control action, replicating previous findings that infants view eating actions as cues that a novel food is edible (e.g., Liberman et al., 2016; Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019).
text.formatted: Infants chose the food they saw an actor eat when this occurred in the context of the touch control action, replicating previous findings that infants view eating actions as cues that a novel food is edible (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Liberman et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wertz & Wynn, 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, although infants differentially attended to the cutting action, our choice data suggest they did not preferentially choose the food they saw an actor cut when this occurred in the context of the touch control action.
One possible explanation is that infants' attention is captured by food processing actions but cues of processing are weaker cues of edibility than eating actions.
In this case, similar designs but with more repetitions of each action might reveal that infants use cues of food processing to guide their food choices as well.

However, when the eating and cutting actions were paired, infants also no longer reliably chose one novel food type over the other, suggesting that context may play a role in how infants make edibility inferences from eating and cutting actions.
There are (at least) two possible interpretations of this pattern of choice results.
First, it may be that the results in the "Eat vs.
Cut" condition represent a failure to replicate the results of the "Eat vs.
Touch" condition, which could cast doubt on the interpretation that infants view eating actions as an indicator of edibility.

However, there is considerable converging evidence that infants and young children view eating actions as an indicator of edibility (e.g., DeJesus et al., 2018; Liberman et al., 2016; Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019), so it is unclear why infants would fail to do so only in the "Eat vs.

text.text: Cut" condition of this study.
Therefore, there is a second possible interpretation.

Specifically, infants may view both the eating and cutting actions as indicators of edibility, but only when the cutting action occurs within the context of other actions that may indicate edibility (like eating actions).
In that case, infants in the "Eat vs.
Cut" condition may not show a preference for one of the two roots when asked "Which one can you eat?"
because they view them both as potentially edible.

Finally, to better understand the factors that may have influenced infants' choices during the Choice Phase, following the suggestion of an anonymous reviewer, we conducted a followup exploratory analysis to examine the relationship between each infant's choice of a particular root and their interest in the preceding action-videos.
Due in large part to the number of "No
Choice" responses in the choice phase, only 37 infants could be included in this analysis across all three conditions and there were no significant relationships within this subset of participants.
Future studies with a larger sample size will be necessary to explore this question in detail.
One potential limitation of our study is that our attempt to closely match our three action types may have made them seem unusual to infants.

For example, we included a tool in all three actions such that the actor first lifted the root with tongs in the eating video, cut the root with a knife in the food processing video, and held the root still with a shoehorn in the touch control video.
While the knife was necessary for the food processing video, it is possible that the presence of an extraneous artifact in the eating and touch action could have been surprising to infants.

Our data suggest that it does not seem to be the case for the eating actions-infants' looking times and pupil dilation were similar across the eating and cutting videos, suggesting that they were not particularly puzzled by the sight of the tongs in the eating video.
However, it may explain infants' longer looking times and greater pupil dilation during the touch control action videos.

Even if this is the case, it suggests that infants were responding to a semantic interpretation of the videos that allowed them to evaluate the plausibility of each action type, rather than lower-level features.

Another limitation of the current study was that, during the Action Presentation Phase of the experiment, the same actor appeared twice on the screen (i.e., performing one action on the left and another action on the right side of the screen).
We chose to have the same actor on all the videos to avoid a potential confound of preference for one person over the other.
It might have been surprising for infants to see the same actor who was alternating in the action videos then duplicated in the action still image.

However, although infants showed interest in the actor's face during the Action Stills, additional follow-up analyses of infants' gaze shifts did not indicate particular attention to the actors' duplicated faces.

Specifically, although infants looked longer at the actor's face area overall, their gaze shifts were distributed similarly between the side-by-side face areas and between other AOIs within the Action Still.
Instead, infants' gaze shifts were roughly equally distributed between all areas of interest.
Finally, a caveat to our choice results is that approximately 40% of infants did not choose any food.
While this is similar to other studies using choice measures with participants in Northern Europe (e.g., Lucca et al., 2025), it reduced our effective sample size and therefore warrants replication.

text.text: Further, we were unable to assess infants' eating behaviors because very few infants attempted to eat the novel food stimuli they had chosen (approximately 25% of infants who made a choice attempted to put the root in their mouths).

Previous work successfully assessed infants' eating behavior in a choice phase using dried fruits (Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019;  although even in these studies, only a subset of infants [approximately 60%] also put the chosen food in their mouth), so it is plausible that infants' lack of eating in the current study was due to the particular novel food stimuli we chose.

text.text: We used white parsnips and black carrots in order to have foods that were obviously unprocessed, unfamiliar to infants, and could be both eaten and cut.

However, infants may have been reluctant to put these root vegetables in their mouths because they were large, hard and did not smell particularly appetizing (unlike fragrant dried fruit) and infants are often offered foods that are cut into pieces at this age.
It is also possible that infants' reluctance to choose reflected a lack of hunger.

Previous studies have found a relationship between 12-month-old infants' hunger levels and their attention to food images, highlighting the need to take this variable into account in future studies (Rioux et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous studies have found a relationship between 12-month-old infants' hunger levels and their attention to food images, highlighting the need to take this variable into account in future studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Rioux et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We did not assess infants' hunger in our study, therefore we cannot rule out this possibility.

Future studies attempting to measure infants' eating behavior could use different unfamiliar food stimuli, including items that are more palatable and account for infants' hunger level prior to testing.
Future studies will be necessary to understand the precise role that food processing actions like cutting play in food learning in infancy.

Specifically, future work could investigate whether a food processing action like cutting indicates edibility per se or something more like the possibility to become edible in the future (e.g., after additional processing steps take place).
Cutting a food is a clear signal of previous human intervention and is interpreted as such by children and adults (e.g., Foroni et al., 2013 , Girgis & Nguyen, 2020).
text.formatted: Cutting a food is a clear signal of previous human intervention and is interpreted as such by children and adults (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Foroni et al., 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">, Girgis & Nguyen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It can also signal intended consumption and modulate edibility evaluations (i.e., whether an item is a food vs. non-food).

For example, Foinant et al. (2021a) found that when 4-to 6-year-old children performed a food vs. non-food categorization task, they were more likely to miscategorize cut non-food items (e.g., pieces of wood) as foods than to miscategorize whole non-food items as foods.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Foinant et al. (2021a)</ref> found that when 4-to 6-year-old children performed a food vs. non-food categorization task, they were more likely to miscategorize cut non-food items (e.g., pieces of wood) as foods than to miscategorize whole non-food items as foods.

text.text: However, a food that is cut into pieces might require further processing before being actually edible (e.g., cassava roots are staple foods in many African countries but have to be cooked to be safely consumed).

It is possible that more advanced processing techniques like cooking, which actually change a food's chemical properties and decrease their potential toxicity (while cutting does not) might be needed to reliably signal edibility.

In the current experiment, we chose cutting a novel food into pieces as a first step because previous work has shown that infants and children behave differently toward cut foods (Foinant et al., 2021a (Foinant et al., , 2021b;; Rioux & Wertz, 2021), but future studies can include more complex food processing techniques.

text.text: Future studies should also investigate how food processing actions may alter infants' representations of food.
Infants expect artificial objects to remain cohesive and are surprised when they break apart (e.g., Shutts et al., 2009; Spelke et al., 1993).
text.formatted: Infants expect artificial objects to remain cohesive and are surprised when they break apart (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Shutts et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Spelke et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: However, their expectations about food are likely to differ.
Infants may not expect foods to remain cohesive because they routinely observe their caregivers transforming food through actions such as cutting, mashing, and cooking.
Additionally, the functional properties of foods are likely more related to internal properties (e.g., nutrients, presence or absence of toxins) than to their shape.

Consistent with this possibility, although infants fail to track object quantity when a food (a cracker) is split into two pieces, they nevertheless maintain a representation of its identity (Cheries et al., 2008), and older children readily accept transformations of food items (e.g., cutting, melting), whereas they are less likely to accept comparable transformations of non-food natural kinds and artifacts (Girgis et al., 2025).

text.text: Another important avenue for future research is to investigate whether the present results are specific to food.
In the current experiment, the root stimuli we used were unfamiliar to infants, so it is likely that they had no prior knowledge of whether the roots were food before any action was shown.
However, it remains an open question whether infants would selectively attend to eating and food processing actions when these actions are performed on any kind of object.
Research on food learning has shown that observing an individual eat an object is a powerful cue of edibility.
For example, Liberman and colleagues (2016) showed that infants interpreted the same artifact object-an opaque bowl-differently depending on the type of action performed on it.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Liberman and colleagues (2016)</ref> showed that infants interpreted the same artifact object-an opaque bowl-differently depending on the type of action performed on it.

text.text: When an adult ate from the bowl with a spoon, infants construed its contents as food; however, they did not do so when the adult simply lifted the bowl.

However, Wertz and colleagues (Rioux & Wertz, 2026; Wertz & Wynn, 2014) showed that infants perceive some objects (i.e., plants) as more likely to be food than others (i.e., artifacts) after observing the same eating actions performed on them.
text.formatted: However, Wertz and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Rioux & Wertz, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wertz & Wynn, 2014)</ref> showed that infants perceive some objects (i.e., plants) as more likely to be food than others (i.e., artifacts) after observing the same eating actions performed on them.

text.text: Future research could use a variety of food and non-food objects to further test the specificity of the effects found in the present study.
Another important question for future research is whether the communicative intent of the person performing the actions is necessary for infants to learn about them.
In our study, the adult greeted and made eye-contact with the infants before performing the action, which are ostensive signals of communication.

Ostensive communication serves the functions of social information exchange and transmission of cultural knowledge during development and infants expect information to be object-centered and generalizable in ostensive contexts (sometimes referred to as natural pedagogy, Csibra & Gergely, 2009; Egyed et al., 2013; Gergely & Kiraly, 2019).
text.formatted: Ostensive communication serves the functions of social information exchange and transmission of cultural knowledge during development and infants expect information to be object-centered and generalizable in ostensive contexts (sometimes referred to as natural pedagogy, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Csibra & Gergely, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Egyed et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gergely & Kiraly, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, infants often passively observe adults and peers eating and processing foods in their daily routine, so it might be that even in non-ostensive contexts (e.g., Kline, 2015) infants use others' actions to learn about food.
text.formatted: On the other hand, infants often passively observe adults and peers eating and processing foods in their daily routine, so it might be that even in non-ostensive contexts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Kline, 2015)</ref> infants use others' actions to learn about food.

text.text: Finally, it is an open question from which social partners infants learn best what to eat.
Infants make social inference based on what they see others eat (e.g., Liberman et al., 2014 Liberman et al., , 2021)), but the impact of social status on food learning in infancy is largely unknown.
text.formatted: Infants make social inference based on what they see others eat (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Liberman et al., 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Liberman et al., , 2021))</ref>, but the impact of social status on food learning in infancy is largely unknown.

text.text: Studies on children's learning from testimony (i.e. others telling them facts about new objects) has shown that children do not treat all informants equally.

Instead, they tend to trust more the information provided by familiar over unfamiliar people, reliable over unreliable, experts over non-experts or nice over mean (Wood et al., 2013; Zmyj et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Instead, they tend to trust more the information provided by familiar over unfamiliar people, reliable over unreliable, experts over non-experts or nice over mean <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Wood et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Zmyj et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, this line of research has mostly been conducted with non-food stimuli and with school-age children and the handful of studies investigating infants and toddlers's food selection based on others' testimonies or actions has revealed mixed findings.

For instance, after watching either a stranger or a familiar adult eating an unfamiliar food, 18-to 30-month-old children accept to eat that food (Addessi et al., 2005; Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019), while in another study, 12-month-old infants prefer to learn from an in-group vs. an out-group member (Shutts et al., 2009).
text.formatted: For instance, after watching either a stranger or a familiar adult eating an unfamiliar food, 18-to 30-month-old children accept to eat that food <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Addessi et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wertz & Wynn, 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2019)</ref>, while in another study, 12-month-old infants prefer to learn from an in-group vs. an out-group member <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Shutts et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies could therefore investigate who has the most influence on infants and toddlers' food selection (e.g., familiar model over unfamiliar, in-group over out-group, etc.).
The present work investigated the actions infants rely on to learn what to eat.

Previous research has shown the influential role of eating actions for guiding infants' food selection (Edelson et al., 2016; Harper & Sanders, 1975; Wertz & Wynn, 2014 , 2019) and our results demonstrate that infants pay similar attention to eating and food processing actions.
text.formatted: Previous research has shown the influential role of eating actions for guiding infants' food selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Edelson et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Harper & Sanders, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wertz & Wynn, 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2019)</ref> and our results demonstrate that infants pay similar attention to eating and food processing actions.

text.text: However, our choice results suggest that infants' food choices are differentially influenced by eating and processing actions depending on the context in which these actions occur.
The strength of the present work is in using converging measures to gain a fuller picture of the cognitive mechanisms underlying infants' food learning.
Our findings can help identify important mechanisms that increase the acceptance of healthy foods early in life.

text.text: In total, 96 infants were tested.

Of these, 10 were initially excluded due to (i) fussiness during the test session (i.e., crying; N = 5), (ii) parental excessive interference during critical phases of the presentation (e.g., pointing to the screen during most of image stills; N = 2), or (iii) inattentiveness (i.e., infants who were not crying but were generally inattentive for most of the experiment; N = 3).

Then, after coding the video sessions to evaluate whether infants attended to critical parts of our displays and if parents interfered during the testing session (see Sections 1.1.1 and 1.1.2 below), and assessing eye-tracking data quality (see Section 1.1.1 below), datasets of additional infants were excluded from the analyses: Some datasets could be excluded from only the eye-tracking analysis or only the choice analysis.
In these cases, infants were retained in the final sample but provided data for only part of the experiment.

The datasets of infants could also be excluded from both the eye tracking and choice analyses (N = 8 exclusions), in which case they were completely excluded from the final sample, resulting in a final sample of N = 78 infants contributing data to at least one part of the study.

text.text: For the cutting action it was when the actor was cutting two slices with the knife -from the point the knife first touches the root to when the knife begins to be lifted away from the root at the end of the second cut.

For the eating action it was when the actor was bringing the root to her mouth and chewing itfrom the point when the mouth first closes on the root until the root is brought away from the lips after the last bite.

For the touching action it was when the actor was touching the root twice with her finger -from the point when the actor's finger first touches the root until her finger begins to be lifted away from the root after the second touch.
2) The infant watched at least 75% of the action video (from when the actor is saying hello to when she looks down at the end).
If the infant briefly looked away it was still acceptable.
We determined that the parent interfered during the action video trial if one of the following situations happened: 1) The parent turned their infant's head and body in the direction of the screen.
2) The parent said to their infant to look at the screen or pointed to the screen.
If the parent soothed their infant because the infant started to show signs of distress, without noticeably drawing away the infant's attention from the screen it was considered as acceptable.
These same criteria for parental interference applied to parental interference during the Root Stills and Action Still.

After trial exclusions due to failure to attend to the videos or parental interference, if fewer than two action video trials remained (one per action type) for a particular infant, the infant was excluded from the final sample because they had not been sufficiently attentive.
Two infants were excluded for this reason.

In addition to our primary analysis, we assessed whether infants' experiences and environment influenced their responses to our stimuli during the experiment.

To do this, we use the data from the battery of five questionnaires that parents filled out assessing their feeding practices as well as their infant's prior food experiences and eating behaviors (Questionnaire 1:

Familiarity with the study stimuli; Questionnaire 2: Food consumption at home; Questionnaire 3: Parental feeding strategies and Infants' eating difficulties; Questionnaire 4: Infants' neophobic behaviors; Questionnaire 5: Socio-demographic characteristics of the family, see details of the questionnaires in the main text, Section 2.4.4).

All correlations between the questionnaire measures and our primary DVs of interest (i.e., looking times towards dynamic actions and image stills, pupil dilation and food choices) are reported in Tables S9-S14 below.

text.text: These correlational analyses revealed that none of the questionnaire measures were systematically related to our DVs of interest.

For instance, with Questionnaires 1 and 2, we assessed whether infants' familiarity with the two roots, or the age of introduction of vegetables in their diet, influenced the average times they spent looking at each dynamic action type (i.e., mean looking time per child across all consecutive trials towards cutting, eating or touching dynamic actions in relation to their prior experiences with the study objects).
Interestingly, almost none of the questions assessing infants' prior experiences with the study objects were related to infants' looking times, pupil dilation or probability to make a choice.

This is in line with previous findings that infants' reaching behaviors and social looking behaviors towards leafy plants and plant foods are not influenced by their' general experience with plants nor their experience with the plant foods they are presented with (Rioux & Wertz, 2021; Wertz & Wynn, 2014; Włodarczyk et al., 2018 Włodarczyk et al., , 2020)).
text.formatted: This is in line with previous findings that infants' reaching behaviors and social looking behaviors towards leafy plants and plant foods are not influenced by their' general experience with plants nor their experience with the plant foods they are presented with <ref type="bibr">(Rioux & Wertz, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wertz & Wynn, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Włodarczyk et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Włodarczyk et al., , 2020))</ref>.

text.text: The absence of a relationship with parental feeding strategies may be due to the content of the Children Feeding and Eating Difficulties questionnaire (Questionnaire 3).

Although the questionnaire assesses caregivers' strategies for overcoming feeding difficulties, it primarily focuses on practices such as scolding and the use of rewards and does not assess social learning strategies, such as parental modeling, closer to what was presented to infants in the current study.
The absence of a relationship with eating difficulties or neophobic behaviors (Questionnaire 4) may reflect a limitation of the present study.
Specifically, we did not obtain a meaningful measure of food consumption because very few infants attempted to eat the roots.
As eating difficulties and food neophobia are primarily expressed during actual eating, their influence may not be reflected in our choice measure.

Finally, regarding parental education (Questionnaire 5), as reviewed by Cole et al., (2017), while some studies found that higher maternal education was associated with a lower risk of picky eating behavior in children (e.g., Migraine et al., 2013), other studies found no such relationship (e.g., Carruth et al., 2004), as was also observed in the present study.
